title: Joshua 17:1–13
context: After Judah (chapter 15) and Ephraim (chapter 16), the allotment turns to the western half of Manasseh. Machir’s line already held Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:39-40). The unit records the clans, the inheritance of Zelophehad’s daughters as Moses had commanded (Numbers 27:1-11), the boundary with Ephraim, and Manasseh’s failure to drive out the Canaanites from several cities.

verses.text: This was the lot for the tribe of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. As for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, because he was a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan.
verses.arminianNotes: Machir received Gilead and Bashan because he was a man of war, so the text links his inheritance to the courage his clan showed in the conquest east of the Jordan. Arminian readers often note how Scripture honors real human faithfulness even within a gift that God freely gives.
verses.reformedNotes: The verse begins with the lot, and Reformed readers stress that the distribution follows God’s ordering rather than tribal strength or merit. Manasseh’s standing as Joseph’s firstborn is noted, though Jacob had placed Ephraim first (Genesis 48:14-20), a reminder that God’s purposes do not simply follow birth order.

verses.text: So this was for the rest of the children of Manasseh according to their families: for the children of Abiezer, for the children of Helek, for the children of Asriel, for the children of Shechem, for the children of Hepher, and for the children of Shemida. These were the male children of Manasseh the son of Joseph according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Six clans are named so that each family can see its place in the inheritance. Arminian readers value this attention to particular households as a sign that God’s promise reaches individual families who must then receive and hold their portion faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: The clan names appear to correspond to the list in Numbers 26:29-33, with small differences in spelling. Reformed readers often see such genealogies as evidence of God’s covenant care for families across generations, keeping his promise to Abraham’s descendants by name.

verses.text: But Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, had no sons, but daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
verses.arminianNotes: Zelophehad had no sons, a situation that could have erased his family from the land. Naming all five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, honors them as real persons with a real claim. Arminian readers see God’s concern that no household be overlooked.
verses.reformedNotes: The genealogy runs back five generations to Manasseh, establishing the daughters’ rightful place in the clan. Reformed readers see God’s law providing for a case that ordinary inheritance customs would have missed, showing that his covenant care extends to the vulnerable.

verses.text: They came to Eleazar the priest, and to Joshua the son of Nun, and to the princes, saying, “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” Therefore according to the commandment of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.
verses.arminianNotes: The daughters appeal directly to the command the LORD gave Moses (Numbers 27:1-11), and their initiative is rewarded. Arminian readers often highlight their bold faith in claiming a promise, an example of believers taking God at his word and asking for what he has pledged.
verses.reformedNotes: Eleazar and Joshua act according to the commandment of the LORD, not their own discretion. Reformed readers stress that the daughters’ claim rests on God’s prior word, and that faithful leaders implement what God has already decreed. Numbers 36 adds that they married within their father’s clan.

verses.text: Ten parts fell to Manasseh, in addition to the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is beyond the Jordan;
verses.arminianNotes: Ten parts fell to Manasseh west of the Jordan, besides Gilead and Bashan. The count is commonly explained as five portions for the male clans and five for Zelophehad’s daughters in place of Hepher. Arminian readers see that the daughters receive a share equal to the other households.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase ten parts fell uses the language of the lot, as if the portions dropped into place by God’s hand. Reformed readers see in it the providence affirmed in Proverbs 16:33, where the lot is cast but every decision is from the LORD.

verses.text: because the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons. The land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator stresses that the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons. Arminian readers find in this a quiet affirmation of the dignity of women within the covenant community and of God’s fairness toward those whom custom might exclude.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse shows God’s law being faithfully carried out across the generation that entered the land. Moses gave the ruling, and Joshua’s generation kept it, so the promise was honored even after the lawgiver died.

verses.text: The border of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethath, which is before Shechem. The border went along to the right hand, to the inhabitants of En Tappuah.
verses.arminianNotes: The border runs from Asher toward Michmethath near Shechem and on toward En Tappuah. The exact course is uncertain for modern readers, but Arminian interpreters see in such detail a God who gives his people a real and defined place to live faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Shechem, near the border, was where God first promised the land to Abram (Genesis 12:6-7). Reformed readers note how the allotment brings that ancient promise into concrete fulfillment, though the precise line of the border cannot be traced with certainty today.

verses.text: The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh; but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim.
verses.arminianNotes: The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself belonged to Ephraim. Arminian readers note that brother tribes had to live with shared boundaries and overlapping claims, a practical setting for patience and cooperation.
verses.reformedNotes: The arrangement shows that tribal borders were not neat, and that God’s distribution could leave towns of one tribe inside another’s territory. Reformed readers see this as one more sign that the allotment was ordered by God rather than drawn for tribal convenience.

verses.text: The border went down to the brook of Kanah, southward of the brook. These cities belonged to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh. The border of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook, and ended at the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: The brook of Kanah marked part of the border, with some Ephraimite cities lying among the cities of Manasseh. Arminian readers see a picture of interdependent tribes, called to live as one people despite the complexity of their inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the text records these details without complaint or adjustment, accepting the boundaries as given. The brook of Kanah is often identified with a stream running west toward the sea, though the identification is not certain.

verses.text: Southward it was Ephraim’s, and northward it was Manasseh’s, and the sea was his border. They reached to Asher on the north, and to Issachar on the east.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim lay to the south and Manasseh to the north, with the sea as the western edge and Asher and Issachar as neighbors. Arminian readers note that each tribe’s portion was set among others, so faithfulness included good relations with neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: The sea as a border echoes the wide promise of land from the river to the great sea (Joshua 1:4). Reformed readers see the allotment of Joseph’s sons as part of God’s faithful fulfillment of that promise, step by step.

verses.text: Manasseh had three heights in Issachar, in Asher Beth Shean and its towns, and Ibleam and its towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and its towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and its towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its towns.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh received towns within Issachar and Asher, including Beth Shean, Taanach, and Megiddo. Arminian readers note that these were strong Canaanite cities, so the gift came with a real challenge that called for courage and trust.
verses.reformedNotes: The meaning of three heights is unclear, and interpreters differ on how to read it. Reformed readers note that several of these cities later became significant in Israel’s history, and they see God placing his people in strategic land, whatever the exact sense of the phrase.

verses.text: Yet the children of Manasseh couldn’t drive out the inhabitants of those cities; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.
verses.arminianNotes: The children of Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants, and the Canaanites were determined to stay. Arminian readers often read this failure as real and consequential, showing that God’s gift could be only partly realized when his people did not fully trust and obey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers take the failure seriously as well, noting that Judges 1:27 repeats it. Many read it as a mark of human weakness and incomplete obedience, while holding that God’s purposes for Israel were not finally defeated by it.

verses.text: When the children of Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, and didn’t utterly drive them out.
verses.arminianNotes: When Israel grew strong, they used the Canaanites for forced labor instead of driving them out. Arminian readers see a choice of convenience over obedience, a compromise that later chapters and Judges show to be costly (Judges 2:1-3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the command had been to drive out these peoples and to make no covenant with them (Deuteronomy 7:1-2). Settling for forced labor reveals divided obedience, and later Scripture traces how such compromise drew Israel toward idolatry.
